e.meaning: something handed down from the past
e.etymology: The English word for what a person leaves to those who come after. It has been used as an American given name in recent decades, alongside Legend and Destiny.

assoc.t: Subaru Legacy, midsize sedan sold 1989 to 2025

e.etymology: From the flowering shrub, whose name comes from Greek azaleos, dry, because it was thought to grow in dry soil.

assoc.t: rapper Iggy Azalea

e.etymology: From the Irish surname O Deasmhumhnaigh, a man from Desmond, the old territory of South Munster in Ireland.
namesakes: Desmond Tutu (South African archbishop and Nobel Peace laureate)
Desmond Doss (WWII medic portrayed in Hacksaw Ridge)

e.etymology: From a surname for a marshal, in Old French mareschal, at first a man who looked after horses and later a high officer of a royal household.
namesakes: Marshall Mathers (the rapper Eminem)
Marshall Eriksen (How I Met Your Mother)

assoc.t: Marshall, the Dalmatian fire pup in PAW Patrol
Marshall guitar amplifiers and speakers
marshal, a law officer, as in US Marshals
Marshalls, off-price clothing and home chain

e.etymology: A 21st-century short form of Gabriella, the feminine of Gabriel, Hebrew for God is my strength.
The Italian feminine of Francesco, from Late Latin Franciscus, Frenchman, the nickname of Saint Francis of Assisi. It is the Italian form of Frances.
namesakes: Francesca Bridgerton (sibling in the Netflix series Bridgerton)
Francesca da Rimini (tragic lover in Dante's Inferno)

e.etymology: From a surname, in Scotland a form of Body or Boddy. Many parents now choose it as a plainer spelling of Bodhi, the Sanskrit word for awakening.

assoc.t: Bodie, California, a gold-rush ghost town

e.etymology: From Latin serena, calm or clear, the name of an early Christian saint.
namesakes: Serena van der Woodsen (Gossip Girl)

assoc.t: tennis champion Serena Williams

e.meaning: a king's son; a royal ruler
e.etymology: The English title, from Old French prince and Latin princeps, first or chief. It has long been both a surname and an occasional American first name.
namesakes: Prince Fielder (MLB slugger)
Prince Royce (bachata singer)

assoc.t: Prince, the Purple Rain musician
Prince tennis rackets

e.meaning: from Kobe, the city in Japan
e.etymology: Kobe Bryant's parents named him in 1978 after Kobe beef, the prized beef from the Japanese city of Kobe. American use of the name has followed his career and rose again after his death in 2020.

assoc.t: Kobe Bryant, Los Angeles Lakers legend
Kobe beef, prized Japanese wagyu
port city in Japan

e.etymology: A Swiss German pet form of Adelheid, noble kind, the source of Adelaide. Johanna Spyri's 1880 children's novel Heidi carried it around the world.
namesakes: Heidi Klum (supermodel and TV host)

assoc.t: orphan girl of the Alps in the classic children's novel

e.etymology: From Old English Eadwine, built on ead, wealth or fortune, and wine, friend. It was the name of a 7th-century king of Northumbria and was revived in the 1800s.
namesakes: Edwin Hubble (astronomer, namesake of the Hubble telescope)
Edwin Aldrin (Buzz Aldrin, second man on the Moon)

e.etymology: From French Gisèle, a short form of Germanic names beginning with gisil, pledge or hostage. The 1841 ballet Giselle made the name known outside France.
namesakes: Gisele Bündchen (Brazilian supermodel, spelled with one l)

assoc.t: Giselle, the Romantic ballet of 1841
Giselle, the princess in Disney's Enchanted

e.meaning: a field of grass and wildflowers
e.etymology: From the English word, Old English maedwe. Its use as a name grew after Meadow Soprano, the daughter on The Sopranos, appeared in 1999.
namesakes: Meadow Soprano (Tony's daughter on The Sopranos)
Meadow Walker (model, daughter of actor Paul Walker)

assoc.t: Meadow Soprano, Tony's daughter on The Sopranos

e.etymology: From the English word sunny, long used as a cheerful nickname and now given in its own right. It is also a pet form of Indian names such as Sunil and Sunita.
namesakes: Sunny Hostin (co-host of The View)
Sunny Baudelaire (baby sister in A Series of Unfortunate Events)

assoc.t: Sunny, the 1966 Bobby Hebb soul hit

e.etymology: From Greek Hektor, 'holding fast', from ekhein, 'to hold'. In the Iliad Hector is the Trojan prince killed by Achilles. In Scotland it also anglicizes the Gaelic name Eachann.
namesakes: Hector (Trojan prince and hero of Homer's Iliad)
Héctor Elizondo (actor, Pretty Woman and The Princess Diaries)
Hector Salamanca (cartel elder in Breaking Bad and Better Call Saul)

assoc.t: Trojan prince and hero of Homer's Iliad
Héctor, the skeleton musician in Pixar's Coco

e.note: As a verb, to hector means to bully or badger.

e.etymology: A pet form of Rose, Rosemary and other rose names, made with the -ie ending. It has long been given as a name in its own right.
namesakes: Rosie O'Donnell (comedian and talk show host)
Rosie Perez (actress, Do the Right Thing)
Rosie Huntington-Whiteley (model and actress)

assoc.t: Rosie the Riveter, World War II home-front icon
Rosie, the robot maid on The Jetsons

e.meaning: jay bird; as an Indian name, victory
e.etymology: In English, a short form of names starting with J such as James and Jason, and a surname taken from the jay bird. As an Indian name it comes from Sanskrit jaya, 'victory'.
namesakes: Jay-Z (rapper and businessman)
Jay Leno (former host of The Tonight Show)
Jay Gatsby (title character of The Great Gatsby)

assoc.t: the jay, the bird family that includes the blue jay

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Schuyler, a Dutch surname meaning 'scholar' that colonial settlers brought to New York. The Skyler spelling has been used since the 1980s.
namesakes: Skyler White (Walter White's wife in Breaking Bad)

e.etymology: From Latin regina, 'queen'. As a given name it first honored the Virgin Mary as Queen of Heaven, and it was the name of an early Christian saint.
namesakes: Regina King (Oscar-winning actress and director)
Regina George (queen bee of Mean Girls)
Regina Hall (actress, Girls Trip)

assoc.t: Regina George, the queen bee in Mean Girls
capital city of Saskatchewan, Canada

e.note: The Canadian city Regina is said ruh-JY-nuh, which rhymes with a body part and draws the occasional joke.

e.etymology: A spelling of Cohen, the Jewish surname from Hebrew kohen, 'priest', borne by families descended from the priestly line of Aaron.
e.note: Kohen is a Jewish priestly title and surname; many Jewish people find it inappropriate as a first name.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yered, usually linked to a root meaning 'to descend'. In Genesis Jared is the father of Enoch. The name was rare in English until the 1960s.
namesakes: Jared Leto (Oscar-winning actor and Thirty Seconds to Mars singer)
Jared Kushner (Trump adviser and son-in-law)
Jared Goff (NFL quarterback)

assoc.t: Jared, the jewelry store chain
Jared Fogle, ex-Subway pitchman jailed for sex crimes

e.note: Former Subway pitchman Jared Fogle, imprisoned for sex crimes in 2015, is still a common reference for the name.

e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Murchadha, 'descendant of Murchadh', a personal name meaning 'sea warrior'. It is the most common surname in Ireland.
namesakes: Murphy Brown (title character of the CBS sitcom)

assoc.t: Murphy's law: anything that can go wrong will
Murphy bed, a bed that folds up into the wall
Murphy USA gas stations
Murphy Oil Soap wood cleaner

e.etymology: From a Scottish and northern English surname meaning 'son of Law', a medieval short form of Lawrence.
A modern spelling of Madeline, from French Madeleine, the name of Mary Magdalene: 'woman of Magdala', a village on the Sea of Galilee whose name means 'tower'.
From the English word for the large black bird, Old English hræfn. It has been used as a given name since the 1970s, often with dark hair in mind.
namesakes: Raven-Symoné (actress, That's So Raven)
Raven (Teen Titans superhero in DC Comics)
Raven Baxter (psychic teen of That's So Raven)

assoc.t: The Raven, Edgar Allan Poe's 1845 poem
Raven, the Teen Titans heroine from DC Comics
That's So Raven, the Disney Channel sitcom

e.etymology: A Scottish and English pet form of James, which goes back to Hebrew Yaakov (Jacob), traditionally 'supplanter'. Since the mid-20th century it has also been given to girls in the US.
namesakes: Jamie Lee Curtis (Oscar-winning actress)
Jamie Foxx (Oscar-winning actor and singer)
Jamie Oliver (British celebrity chef)

e.etymology: A 1990s American coinage in the style of Jaylen and Kayla, joining the Jay- sound to the -la ending.

e.meaning: of Mars, the Roman god of war
e.etymology: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Mark, from Latin Marcus, which is thought to derive from Mars, the Roman god of war.
namesakes: Marco Polo (Venetian explorer of Asia)
Marco Rubio (US senator and secretary of state)

assoc.t: Marco Polo, the call-and-answer swimming pool game

e.etymology: From Late Latin Laura, the feminine of laurus, 'laurel tree', the ancient emblem of victory. Petrarch's 14th-century sonnets to his beloved Laura made the name famous.
namesakes: Laura Ingalls Wilder (author of Little House on the Prairie)
Laura Bush (former First Lady)
Laura Dern (Oscar-winning actress)

assoc.t: hurricane that struck Louisiana in 2020

e.etymology: From an English surname based on Old French traverser, 'to cross', given to someone who collected tolls at a bridge or crossing.
namesakes: Travis Kelce (Kansas City Chiefs tight end)
Travis Scott (rapper)
Travis Barker (Blink-182 drummer)

e.etymology: A Latinate form of Adeline, a pet form of Adela, from the Germanic word adal, 'noble'. It is the usual form in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese.
